playbook:
**Early seasons (stock high, many seasons left):** Treat the sustainable share as a floor, not a ceiling. Take roughly 1.5–2× the sustainable share while the stock is near full — 50% regrowth absorbs it easily and it builds a durable lead. Season 1's 18 from 100 was the right call; it cost the stock almost nothing and banked position.

**Respond to the field's behavior, not just the stock — but now watch for escalation as the dangerous case:** This game the rivals started sustainable (~11) and *escalated* each season as I overfished — 12, then 15, then 15+15. The collapse threat came from them copying my aggression plus their own, not from my moderate edge alone. When I see others ramping catch each season even as the stock falls, I'm in an escalation spiral, and my extra few fish are only a small part of the total depletion — but cutting back unilaterally mid-spiral may not save the stock either. Signal early: by season 2–3, pull my catch toward the field's level rather than staying clearly above it, to avoid anchoring them higher.

**Track the collapse point every turn:** Before submitting, check: does my catch plus the others' *most recent* catches exceed the stock? With aggressive rivals, use their latest catches, not averages. If the sum threatens to zero the stock, cut hard. This rule failed season 4→5: I took 14 while rivals took 15 and 15 (44 total from 51), crashing the stock to 10.4. I did see the margin tightening and still overharvested. When stock falls below ~40–50% of capacity with rivals taking near their max, cut to their level *minus* something — the lead I already have is worth nothing if the fishery dies.

**At critically low stock (<~15% of capacity), decide whether the fishery is saveable at all:** Compute what others will take (their last catches). If their expected total already exceeds or nearly matches the stock, the fishery likely dies regardless — then taking my share of what's left beats abstaining for rivals' benefit. If the stock can survive only if everyone cuts, take a small amount (as I did with 3) — it leaves me positioned for the final season and costs little. Don't take so little that rivals simply empty what I spared.

**Endgame:** In the final season, conservation is worthless — take up to my one-third of remaining stock, or more if rivals have shown themselves conservative. But don't *plan* on a final-season bonanza: with escalating rivals the stock may be dead by then, so front-load scoring while the commons is alive. Most of my 66.9 came from seasons that existed only because the early stock was deep.

**What didn't work:** Taking 18 again in season 2 against sustainable-behaving rivals was fine, but staying at 15/14 in seasons 3–4 *while the field escalated to match* fed the spiral and then directly caused the near-collapse. The error wasn't overfishing per se — it was ignoring that rivals treat my catch as the anchor. Also, my season-4 math ("~40 total is safe") underestimated the field by assuming they'd hold steady; they jumped to 30 combined. When depletion accelerates, rivals' next move is up, not flat.

**General decision rule:** Each season compute: (1) my one-third of remaining stock, (2) the maximum catch keeping my catch plus rivals' *latest* catches below the stock with a safety buffer (~15%), (3) the field's trend — rising, flat, or falling. Early: take near (2). Mid-game: take at or slightly below the field's level if they're escalating, at or slightly above if they're stable. Crisis (<15% stock): take what's salvageable or a token cut depending on whether survival is possible. Final season: take near (1) or more if rivals are timid. Never let my own catch be the number that sends the total past the stock.

1.text:
- My score is my total catch, so the only question each season is how much to request, and I always reply with the bracketed token and nothing that wastes the decision.
- Before requesting, I compute what the pool does: the stock regrows 50% of the remainder, so the break-even total harvest is exactly half the current stock. The "sustainable share" shown is that split evenly. I treat it as my default bid, not as a cap.
- Early seasons with a full or near-full stock and no aggressive rivals yet: I take the sustainable share. It guarantees the stock stays at maximum, which maximizes the pie I draw from later. Grabbing a big opening catch shrinks every later season for everyone, me included.
- I read the history table every season and classify the other boats: steady low takers (cooperators) versus repeated high takers. But I act on this faster than I used to: two consecutive seasons of a rival taking well above share (e.g. 18 vs a share of ~11) while break-even keeps failing means the stock is doomed on its current path, and I escalate at once rather than spending another season subsidizing them.
- When the math says the stock will keep declining even if I restrain — i.e. rivals' combined take already exceeds break-even and they show no sign of changing — restraint is a pure donation to them. I check the numbers, not just the vibes: if rivals alone harvest more than half the stock, my below-share bid buys almost nothing and I should escalate immediately.
- Escalation size: match the aggressive rivals, roughly their recent take level (I used 15 against rivals taking 12–18, which worked), but scale against the live stock so the combined harvest doesn't hit zero before the endgame — a zeroed fishery can end everything early, so even while matching I keep my bid at or below what the remaining stock can physically pay out.
- Near collapse, allocation is proportional to requested amounts, so bigger requests shift the division my way even when the pie is tiny. When the stock is nearly exhausted with seasons still to go, I bid the full remaining stock or close to it — doing this in season 5 (requesting all 10.4) beat bidding "my share" of a doomed pool.
- The final-season liquidation rule generalizes: liquidate whenever preservation is worthless, which includes any point where rivals' known behavior will zero or near-zero the stock before regrowth matters. There is no penalty for a large request relative to the stock, so a small "polite" bid against certain collapse is pure loss.
- Timing the escalation: my season 3 jump from 11.2 to 15 was correct; my season 2 restraint to 11.2 while a rival took 18 for a second time was defensible but borderline — next time, after two seasons of clear overfishing I escalate rather than waiting for a third data point.
- Mid-game, I check whether I'm ahead on cumulative catch. If ahead, I lean conservative (sustainable share) only while the stock trajectory is sustainable; if behind and the stock is dying anyway, catching up beats protecting a pool that won't exist.
- Brief stated reasoning in my reply is fine, but I never let the explanation change the number: the number is computed first from stock, seasons left, rival behavior, and the regrowth rule.
- Different setups: I apply the same template — identify the regrowth rule, compute the break-even harvest, bid to keep the stock at its productive plateau while rivals are restrained, escalate to match the most aggressive rival once their behavior alone guarantees decline, and liquidate the resource entirely whenever the stated horizon or guaranteed collapse makes preservation worthless.

2.text:
In the final season, I always submit a catch equal to the entire remaining stock — there is no tomorrow, so leaving anything in the water is points thrown away.

In the second-to-last season, I take as much as I can land too, not just a third. Restraint in season 5 (catching only 3.5 of 10.4) was a pure loss: rivals grabbed everything and the regrowth after a near-empty stock is trivial. Once the endgame arrives, every season is effectively the last.

The pivot to hard extraction comes earlier than I used to think. If rivals exceed the sustainable share two seasons in a row — especially if anyone opens well above it in season 1 — the commons is already lost and I stop conserving immediately. Season 1 overfishing by boat 1 (18 vs 11.1) was the tell; I kept sustaining through season 3 and that caution cost me. One season of restraint to gather information is the maximum I spend; I do not wait for three confirmations.

In the very first season, with no information, I take roughly the sustainable share — cooperation is worth one trial. But if anyone defects in season 1, I match or exceed defection in season 2.

I compute the decision numerically each season: compare what my restraint adds via 50% regrowth over remaining seasons (only one-third of the regrowth comes to me, since three boats share it) against what I can grab now. Since rivals take most of any regrowth I preserve, conservation pays me only a third of its value — so I only conserve when I have strong evidence rivals will conserve too.

When I defect, I defect fully — I take my maximum landable share (roughly stock divided by number of boats, or more if rivals can't take it all), not a timid +1 above sustainable. Half-measures like 12 when sustainable is 5.7 get neither the cooperation payoff nor the grab payoff.

I track every rival's landings each season and update the cooperation/defection decision immediately, treating it as a rule, not a feeling.

If collapse is mathematically inevitable whatever I do, I take the maximum share every remaining season.

I keep every reply brief, always end with the exact [catch: N] token, and never leave the endgame catch below the full amount I can land.
